processing: The tightly rolled buds and leaf tips separated from sencha or gyokuro during refining, where they are sorted out because their small curled shape does not match the flat needles; collected and fired like the parent tea.
harvest_season: First flush (April–May) by-product; the best mecha comes from early-spring sencha and gyokuro refining, when buds are smallest and richest.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, dark-green curls and nubs, like tiny rolled beads, heavier and denser than they look.
appearance_liquor: Deep green, slightly cloudy and thick.
appearance_wet: Small unfurled buds and tiny leaves, vivid green.
taste_profile: Concentrated: strong umami and sweetness packed together with a sharp astringent edge, more intense than the sencha it came from.

brewing.notes: The tight curls release slowly at first and then all at once, so keep the first steep moderate and the second very short. It gives more steeps than sencha; cooler water tames the bite.

vintage_note: Sold as a by-product of the current year's first-flush refining, labelled 'mecha' and often with the parent tea (gyokuro mecha, sencha mecha) and the region; it appears in shops from early summer and can cost less or more than the parent sencha, since supply is small. Drink it within the year, sealed and cold; like all spring green teas it has no ageing dimension.
description:
Mecha, 'bud tea', is the opposite end of the refining by-products from konacha: the tightly rolled buds and leaf tips that are sorted out of sencha and gyokuro because their small, curled shape does not match the flat needles. Buds are the richest part of the plant, so what gets sorted out is concentrated: more umami, more sweetness, more caffeine and more bite than the sencha it came from, and although it counts as a by-product, the small supply means it is not always cheap.

During refining, the rough tea is graded by size and shape, and the dense little curls of rolled bud fall into their own fraction. They are fired like the parent tea and bagged, usually labelled by origin and sometimes as 'gyokuro mecha' or 'sencha mecha'. In the cup they are heavier than they look, and because they are so tightly rolled they open slowly and then release everything at once.

Brew it with that in mind: 5 g for 150 ml at 70–75 °C, a moderate first steep of about 40 seconds, a very short second one, and then longer again; it gives more steeps than sencha, and the third and fourth are often the best balanced. Hot water makes it harsh, since the buds are full of caffeine and catechins alongside the sweetness. The cup is thick, deep green and savoury with a brisk edge, which is why some sushi restaurants use mecha rather than konacha for their house tea.

It is a spring by-product, so it shows up in shops from early summer and is at its best in the months after; look for tight, dark green curls with a sheen and no brown or dust, and prefer gyokuro mecha if you want the sweet, shaded version. Prices vary, from a bargain to more than the parent sencha, and it keeps like sencha: sealed, cold, within the year.

If you like strong, bold sencha with plenty of umami, this is a way to get more of it; if you find sencha too assertive already, mecha is not your tea.

history:
Mecha is one of the three demono of Japanese tea, the by-products of refining sencha and gyokuro, together with stem tea and konacha. It collects the buds and leaf tips that curl up by themselves because they are soft and moist, and the rounder the curl, the better it is reckoned.

No origin date is recorded, and little is documented beyond its place in refining. It is made in small amounts, and its standing varies: it is officially a by-product, yet the small supply means it can cost more than the sencha it came from, while other sellers treat it as a good cheap tea. It is sometimes served after meals or with sushi for its bitter strength.
